## Design assessment

Keep these questions in mind:

-   ***Reproducibility:*** could someone rerun the analysis and obtain the same results?

-   ***Transparency:*** can we identify the choices that affect the results?

-   ***Replicability:*** would a new sample lead to a similar protein panel and predictive performance?

::: notes
Introduce the questions briefly. Save the broader discussion for after the guest block so it does not consume the reserved time.
:::

## An alternative analysis

Our earlier approach separated:

1.  selecting proteins
2.  fitting logistic regression using the selected proteins

. . .

***LASSO combines variable selection and coefficient estimation.***

It is useful here because we have many more candidate proteins than subjects.

## LASSO: brief review

For logistic regression, penalize the negative log-likelihood:

$$
(\hat{\beta}_0,\hat{\beta})=
\arg\min_{\beta_0,\beta}
\left\{-\ell(\beta_0,\beta;x,y)+\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}|\beta_j|\right\}.
$$

-   The penalty shrinks coefficients and can set some exactly to zero

-   Larger $\lambda$ generally produces a sparser model

-   The intercept is not penalized

::: notes
Treat this as review for students who took PSTAT 131. The reference slides provide a toy example and further explanation for those who need it.
:::

## Selecting the penalty

Use cross-validation ***within the training data*** to compare penalty values.

-   `lambda.min`: smallest mean cross-validated loss

-   `lambda.1se`: largest penalty within one standard error of that minimum

. . .

For this example, use `lambda.1se` and then evaluate the chosen model on the held-out test set.

The test set does not choose the penalty or the proteins.

## The biomarker workflow

1.  Split subjects into training and test sets

2.  Use training data to tune the penalty and fit the LASSO classifier

3.  Examine which proteins have nonzero coefficients

4.  Evaluate the chosen model on the held-out subjects

. . .

***Scaling and other learned preprocessing belong inside the training procedure.***

::: notes
This is the handoff point. Feel free to use this familiar analysis if it is helpful. The complete example is in the reference section.
:::

## Returning to the analysis

Look back at your diagram and discuss:

-   What would another team need to reproduce your results?

-   Which choices could change the selected protein panel?

-   What evidence would support a claim about performance on new subjects?

::: notes
Keep this to about five minutes. If relevant, invite students to connect something from the guest session to these questions, without assuming that particular tools or examples were covered.
:::

## Some final thoughts

-   Reproducing a computation and validating a predictive model address different questions

-   Similar prediction accuracy can accompany different selected protein panels

-   A small test set gives an uncertain estimate of future performance

-   Neither variable selection nor classification accuracy alone establishes diagnostic usefulness

## Concepts and skills

-   Multiple testing and protein selection

-   Classification using logistic regression and random forests

-   LASSO regularization and cross-validation

-   Reproducible analysis and evaluation on held-out data

<!-- # Reference slides {.appendix} -->

<!-- ## Why regularization? -->

<!-- With more predictors than observations, ordinary unpenalized logistic regression does not provide a uniquely identified coefficient vector and may also suffer from separation. -->

<!-- The LASSO penalty constrains coefficient size and can produce a sparse model. -->

<!-- . . . -->

<!-- Sparsity does not guarantee that the selected proteins are the true biological drivers or that selection will be stable across samples. -->

<!-- ## Constrained and penalized forms -->

<!-- One formulation constrains the coefficient vector: -->

<!-- $$ -->

<!-- \underset{\beta_0,\beta}{\operatorname{maximize}}\; -->

<!-- \ell(\beta_0,\beta;x,y) -->

<!-- \quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{j=1}^{p}|\beta_j|\leq t. -->

<!-- $$ -->

<!-- A corresponding penalized formulation is -->

<!-- $$ -->

<!-- \underset{\beta_0,\beta}{\operatorname{minimize}}\; -->

<!-- -\ell(\beta_0,\beta;x,y)+\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}|\beta_j|. -->

<!-- $$ -->

<!-- The intercept is excluded from the constraint and penalty. -->

<!-- LASSO: @tibshirani1996regression -->
